extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical literature, textual criticism, and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and practical principles drawn from Aristotle's Poetics (with commentary) for understanding, composing, and critiquing poetry—especially tragedy—including classification (medium/theme/mode), what poetry portrays, and textual-critical rules for emendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence of Poetry (portrayal/imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The genus of Art is 'portrayal,' literally 'imitation'; poetry is defined as 'portrayals of the imaginary' (as distinct from history which portrays the actual). The Essence is given by the formula which, without containing the word itself, gives the self of the thing named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that poetry fabricates/simulates (poiesis) and generalizes; its object is the typical/universal rather than particular facts. This is the foundational definition from which other rules flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special functions of varieties (function corresponds to species)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each variety (e.g. Tragedy, Comedy, Epic, Dithyrambic) has its special function, and the function corresponds to the species—as in other arts where each individual has a role (Politics analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or analysing, identify the specific function tied to the genre/species and let that determine structural and stylistic choices (members, factors, treatment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetically correct is not identical with morally correct
rubrics_metrics.description: Being 'poetically correct' (i.e. correct by the principles of poetic art) is not the same as being morally correct or correct by the standards of some other science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject poetic choices merely because they conflict with moral or scientific correctness; judge them by poetic principles (e.g., plausibility within the imaginary, unity, representation of types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Members and factors analysis (tragedy vs epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific knowledge of a work is obtained by analysis into factors or anatomy into members. In the Poetics both divisions are employed for Tragedy (members and factors); Epic receives factorial analysis only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tragedy, analyse both the constituent parts (plot, character, thought, diction, song, spectacle) and the functional relations (how each factor contributes). For epic prioritise structural/factor analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three bases of classification: Clothing, Theme, Treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayals differ in three matters—Clothing (category/medium), Theme (species of subject), and Treatment (mode of presentation). These are arranged in order of importance and can cross-divide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating/assessing a poetic work, specify (1) medium (rhythm/language/harmony), (2) the moral/intellectual type of subject (good/bad/average), and (3) whether it is narrated or impersonated; choices on each axis shape the work's genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothing / medium selection: rhythm, language, harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic 'clothing' (medium) is what clothes the creations—rhythm, language and harmony—which may be used separately or mixed (e.g., verse = language+rhythm; music = harmony+dance). Different media appeal to different faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose media appropriate to the effect and faculty you aim to move. Be aware that mixing media (e.g., sung drama) creates hybrid effects and that some media (dance, instrumental music) simulate differently from language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme: choice of species (typical characters/subjects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Themes vary by species—when fully conscious beings are simulated there is a natural division into good, bad and average. Poetry aims at the typical (the species) not the merely actual individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects that exemplify a type (a typical fate or moral situation) rather than over-specific incidents; the successful poetic subject isolates qualities governed by moral or natural 'laws' so the work has universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment (mode): narration vs impersonation
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment varies in mode—narration and impersonation (dramatic enactment) are distinct modes of speech and presentation, affecting how the audience experiences the imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to tell (narrate) or show (impersonate). Impersonation (drama) offers immediacy and mimicry; narration permits summary and different scope. The mode should suit the genus and aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of the imaginary / focus on the potential and typical
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry portrays the imaginary—events as they might be under moral certainty or laws of nature—isolating qualities to display a coherent, typical course; poetry treats what is possible and probable, not necessarily actual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots that render plausible chains of cause/effect within the world's moral/natural laws; use idealized situations that reveal essences rather than attempting documentary realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal (artistic) vs realistic (familiar) portrait
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'ideal' or artistic portrait assembles the best traits from individuals into a typical figure (Zeuxis selecting traits for Helen); the 'realistic' portrait represents an individual as he is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use idealization when you want the character to embody a type or virtue; use realistic portrayal when individual particularity matters. Recognize that idealization increases universal resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy portrays action/career (faring) rather than mere character
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy portrays not imaginary men but an imaginary 'faring' (a career/happiness); the career (what happens to the person) is the predominant element, character being secondary and often inferred from actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing tragedy, build the plot around a coherent trajectory (career/faring) that embodies the tragic type; characters should be defined by their choices and fortunes within that trajectory (coin analogy: genus precedes differentia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute interdependence of parts (unity and design)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan on which a Tragedy should be arranged is the absolute interdependence of all the parts; Aristotle's treatise itself follows a carefully interdependent plan, and rearrangement risks havoc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plots so each incident and scene contributes indispensably to the whole (unity of action). Avoid gratuitous episodes or structural tinkering that breaks logical/causal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and dance function: measures simulate experiences and emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm (especially for dance) and dance-measures portray not only moral qualities but emotions and experiences; dancing can render hunting, war, work, and other activities mimetically via footed and figured measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In performance writing or dramaturgy, consider choreography and rhythmic patterns as conveyors of meaning and emotion, not mere ornament. For text-only poetry, rhythm (metre) can perform analogous mimetic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony/melody as counterfeit of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmony (understood as tune/melody rather than chords) counterfeits character; melody imitates psychic motion and can suggest moods or moral qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use melodic or prosodic patterns to evoke character traits or emotions. In verse, attend to melodic qualities of language (euphony, cadence) as part of characterization and mood-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis: reproductive (copy) vs creative (generalizing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproductive art copies the actual (figure, colour, sound as likeness); creative art (poetry) fabricates and generalizes—suggestion rather than exact replication. Both work by different mechanisms of audience association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether your aim is faithful reproduction (documentary realism) or creative generalization (universal truth). Use associative detail strategically in reproductive modes; rely on synthesis and typification in creative modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual-criticism principles for emendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before accepting any emendation of a carefully constructed text ask: Does it violate Greek usage? Does it disagree with the author's system? Does it make the author say or suggest anything which he wished to avoid? Amateur alteration spreads havoc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply ruthless, principled tests (usage, systemic consistency, authorial intent) to any proposed correction. Prefer restraint; accept emendations only when they improve syntax/argument without breaking the author's system. Be wary of later translations or interpolations that may reflect different theories rather than original meaning.
